name: Seedborn Reach

stars.name: Seedborn
stars.notes: Ancient orange dwarf, one of the oldest known stars hosting complex life. Its longevity has permitted extraordinarily deep evolutionary development on its habitable world.

planets.name: Rootfire
planets.notes: Tidally locked volcanic world. Lava flows on the dayside create a permanent infrared glow visible to instruments throughout the inner system.

planets.name: Oldgrowth
planets.notes: Ancient garden world with an unbroken evolutionary lineage spanning over 4 billion years. Continent-spanning fungal networks may represent the oldest living organisms in known space. Population 85 million in carefully managed research settlements.

planets.name: Dusthusk
planets.notes: Dry, atmosphere-stripped world. Fossil evidence suggests microbial life existed here over 3 billion years ago before the atmosphere was lost.

planets.name: Icehollow
planets.notes: Frozen outer world with a subsurface ocean. Thermal vents detected but not yet explored by crewed missions.

planets.name: Fardim
planets.notes: Small ice body at the system's edge. Hosts an automated communications relay for deep space exploration missions.

asteroid_belts.name: The Spore Drift
asteroid_belts.notes: Contains trace biological material consistent with Oldgrowth's fungal biochemistry. May represent ancient impact ejecta carrying viable spores.

stations.name: Oldgrowth Orbital
stations.notes: Premier xenobiology research station. Visiting scientists must undergo six-month quarantine protocols before surface access is granted.

stations.name: Seedgate
stations.notes: Entry checkpoint for all traffic entering the system. Biosecurity screening is mandatory; no exceptions are granted.

faction_control.notes: Scientific governance body with strict population caps and development limits. The entire system is classified as a Protected Biosphere Reserve under interstellar treaty.

history: Discovered in 2296 by a deep-range survey mission that detected anomalous biosignatures from Oldgrowth—the spectral signatures of a biosphere far older and more complex than any previously cataloged.
The Oldgrowth Research Authority was established by interstellar treaty in 2304, granting the system protected status and limiting human presence to minimize ecological disruption.

In 2318, researchers identified continent-spanning fungal networks on Oldgrowth estimated at over 2 billion years old, making them the oldest known living organisms and triggering a wave of scientific pilgrimage to the system.
description: Seedborn Reach is a system of deep time. Its orange star has burned for over eight billion years—nearly twice Sol's current age—and in that vast span, the world of Oldgrowth has developed a biosphere of staggering complexity and antiquity. The planet is not the most visually dramatic garden world in known space; its forests are dark and ancient, its megafauna cautious and slow-moving, its oceans deep and still. But beneath the surface, fungal networks spanning continents have been growing, connecting, and exchanging chemical signals for over two billion years. Some xenobiologists argue these networks constitute a form of distributed intelligence—not sentient, but aware in ways that defy easy categorization.

Human presence in Seedborn Reach is deliberately minimal. The Oldgrowth Research Authority limits the system's population to under 100,000, nearly all of whom are scientists, support staff, and their families. There are no cities on Oldgrowth—only small research settlements built on elevated platforms to minimize contact with the fungal networks below. Visitors must undergo months of biosecurity screening before they are permitted to set foot on the surface. The system receives a steady stream of researchers from across known space, but commerce is virtually nonexistent. What Seedborn Reach offers cannot be bought: the chance to study life that has been evolving uninterrupted for longer than Earth has existed.

The deepest question in Seedborn Reach concerns the fungal networks themselves. They respond to stimuli in coordinated ways that span thousands of kilometers. They alter soil chemistry to favor certain plant species over others across entire continents. When researchers introduced a novel chemical compound to a small test area, the network rerouted growth patterns across a 200-kilometer radius within days—an apparent immune response at a planetary scale. If Oldgrowth's fungal networks are truly intelligent, even in a rudimentary sense, the implications for how humanity defines life and consciousness are profound. The answer may take decades more to determine, but in a system measured in billions of years, decades are nothing.
